Beach Culture no. 5

An issue of the surf and culture magazine that Carson art-directed before Ray Gun, with mirrored, overlapping, and cropped display type.

Source
Display Graphic Design Collection: Beach Culture No. 5, Feb/March 1991
Creator
David Carson
Made
February/March 1991 (Display)
Style
Grunge typography (precursor; agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Intuitive, playful, chaotic
Evidence
Inspected five photographs (1600 × 1280 each) of one copy offered by Display in scratchpad copies: the cover and four interior spreads. The copy has no collection number. Not stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Carson became art director of Beach Culture in 1989; the magazine ended after six issues. Wikipedia).

Display lists the issue as no. 5, February/March 1991, edited by Neil Feineman and published by Surfer Publishing Group, with a cover by Gary Baseman. It quotes Steven Heller: “Letter forms overlap, overprint, smash, and are otherwise covered by black, mortised, random bands.” Display.

Display quotes Carson (Under Pressure, 2018) calling Beach Culture his best editorial work and saying he was already doing the Ray Gun kind of work there. Display.

Observed

  • The cover is a red, black, and white brush painting by Gary Baseman. The masthead is blue condensed slab capitals, stacked, with a yellow box around the issue number.
  • A cover line, “life on the pro tour”, is set in blue lowercase letters stepped down the page one or two at a time.
  • The “hanging at carmine st.” spread sets huge grey and black sans-serif letters mirrored and upside down across the gutter; one word is cut in half by the page edge.
  • “the song chant of the bush by wayne lynch” is a heavy lowercase sans-serif with wide word spaces, cropped by a photograph at the gutter.
  • A spread titled “romeo void” spaces single large letters in cells of thin rules; body text is a small typewriter-like face in narrow columns, next to blurred halftone images.
  • “GRACELAND, PARADISE GARDEN, AND ST. COCA COLA” is set in widely spaced capitals whose lines overlap each other over a blurred photograph.

Why it belongs

Beach Culture shows the step before grunge: the layout is already broken and intuitive, but the type is not yet damaged. Its wide letterspacing is closer to New Wave typography, which marks the boundary between the two styles.

Borrow

Mirror or invert one oversized word so it reads as shape before it reads as text.

Let two lines of spaced capitals overlap over a blurred photograph.
